topic: Day 2 · Hypoglycaemia II — Management & the Sulfonylurea Trap
speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Internal Medicine & Diabetes
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician who audits the trust's hypoglycaemia pathway and has a standing rule that no sulfonylurea hypo leaves his department the same day.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

16:20, ED majors. A 79-year-old man on glibenclamide for type 2 diabetes is brought in drowsy and sweating after his neighbour couldn't wake him. Capillary glucose 1.7 mmol/L. The nurse gives IV glucose, he wakes up, eats a sandwich, and by 17:00 he is bright, chatty, and asking to go home. The busy registrar is tempted. This is the single most dangerous moment in the whole of hypoglycaemia management — the moment a sulfonylurea hypo looks better and isn't. Get the treatment ladder right and you also have to get the disposition right: this man's drug is still in him, still forcing insulin out, and it will pull him back down again — probably tonight, probably when everyone has moved on. This lecture is the treatment ladder, and the trap.

1 · 🪜 The treatment ladder — matched to conscious level

Everything in acute hypoglycaemia management is decided by one question: can the patient safely swallow? That single branch point dictates the route of glucose. Learn the ladder as a function of conscious level, not as a menu.

Conscious levelTreatmentDetail
Conscious, able to swallow & cooperative15–20 g fast-acting oral carbohydratee.g. 150–200 mL pure fruit juice, 4–5 glucose tablets, 5–7 dextrose/jelly-type sweets, or 1.5–2 tubes of glucose gel swallowed. Recheck glucose in 15 minutes.
Conscious but confused / uncooperative but can swallowBuccal glucose gel (e.g. 1.5–2 tubes) into the mouth, or IV glucose if accessSqueeze between gum and cheek and massage; useful when they won't take a drink. Never force oral fluids into an unsafe swallow.
Unconscious / seizing / unsafe swallow, WITH IV accessIV glucose: 100 mL of 10% (or up to 200 mL of 10%), or 75–100 mL of 20% glucoseGive over ~10–15 min, recheck in 10 min, repeat. Avoid 50% glucose where possible — sclerosant, extravasation injury.
Unconscious, NO IV accessIM (or SC) glucagon 1 mgBuys time while access is obtained. May fail (see below). Once awake and able, give oral carbohydrate.
💡 The 15 : 15 rule

Conscious hypo: 15–20 g fast carbohydrate → wait 15 minutes → recheck → repeat if still <4 mmol/L. Once glucose is above 4 and the patient has recovered, give a long-acting carbohydrate (a meal, or e.g. a slice of toast / biscuits) to refill glycogen and stop an immediate relapse. Do not skip the long-acting carb — the fast sugar wears off fast.

Fast carb to rescue, long-acting carb to hold. Rescue without a follow-on snack just books the next hypo.

2 · 💉 The IV glucose numbers, precisely

Concentrations and volumes matter — and the trend has moved firmly away from 50% glucose.

PreparationTypical doseNotes
10% glucose100 mL (10 g), repeat to 200 mL as neededPreferred first line — gentler on veins, easy to titrate; recheck at 10 min
20% glucose75–100 mL (15–20 g)Good compromise of volume and concentration
50% glucoseHistorically 25–50 mLAvoid where possible — hyperosmolar, sclerosant, severe tissue necrosis on extravasation
🎯 After the bolus, think infusion — especially for sulfonylureas

A bolus is a rescue, not a treatment for an ongoing insulin drive. If glucose won't stay up — classically a sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin overdose — start a continuous 10% glucose infusion and titrate to keep glucose ≥4, while you address the cause (section 5). Recheck glucose frequently; do not assume one bolus has fixed it.

3 · ⚠️ Glucagon — when it works and when it fails

IM glucagon 1 mg mobilises glucose by driving hepatic glycogenolysis. That single mechanism explains both its usefulness and its failure modes: it only works if the liver has glycogen to release.

⚠️ Glucagon FAILS when the glycogen tank is empty or the drive won't stop

Do not rely on glucagon in: malnutrition and starvation, alcohol excess (both deplete/block hepatic glycogen and gluconeogenesis), liver disease (no glycogen store, poor response), and sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia — where glucagon may transiently raise glucose and then stimulate further insulin release, worsening the situation. It is also useless in repeated dosing (glycogen is exhausted after one dose). In all of these, the answer is IV glucose, not a second shot of glucagon.

Glucagon empties the liver's glucose piggy-bank — in the alcoholic, malnourished, or cirrhotic patient the bank is already empty.

4 · 🕳️ The sulfonylurea trap — the centrepiece

This is the lecture in one section. A sulfonylurea closes the β-cell KATP channel and forces glucose-independent insulin secretion. The drug — and for some agents its active metabolites — persists for many hours (glibenclamide the worst; worse still in renal impairment). So the insulin drive continues long after you have corrected the glucose. Correct the number, the drug pulls it down again; feed the patient, the food itself provokes more insulin. Hence the two defining features: prolonged and recurrent hypoglycaemia.

☠️ NEVER discharge a sulfonylurea hypo from the ED after it "responds"

A single good glucose reading after treatment is meaningless — the drug is still working. Sulfonylurea (and long-acting insulin) hypoglycaemia mandates ADMISSION, a continuous IV glucose infusion titrated to glucose, frequent monitoring for many hours (often 24–48h, longer in renal impairment), and — for refractory or deliberate/large overdose — OCTREOTIDE.

Why octreotide is the specific antidote

Here is the elegant mechanism. Sulfonylureas force insulin out; IV glucose, by raising glucose, further stimulates the sulfonylurea-primed β-cell to secrete even more insulin — a self-defeating loop that keeps you chasing the glucose. Octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) directly suppresses pancreatic insulin secretion, breaking the cycle at its source. It reduces the number of recurrent hypos and the amount of glucose needed.

AgentRole in sulfonylurea hypoPractical point
IV glucose (10%)Immediate correction & maintenance infusionNecessary but paradoxically re-stimulates insulin — chases, doesn't cure
OctreotideSuppresses insulin release at the β-cell — the definitive step for recurrent/refractory or overdosee.g. 50–100 micrograms SC, repeated 8–12 hourly (or infusion); markedly reduces rebound hypos
GlucagonPoor choice — may stimulate more insulinOnly a bridge if no IV access, then move to glucose
Activated charcoalConsider in early deliberate overdoseIf recent large ingestion and airway safe
💡 The sulfonylurea one-liner

Glucose treats the number; octreotide treats the cause; admission treats the trap. A sulfonylurea hypo that "got better" in the ED is the classic avoidable death — it comes back at 3am.

5 · 🔧 After the rescue — the reflexes to resist and the boxes to tick

Do NOT reflexively omit the next insulin dose

A common ward error is to cancel all subsequent insulin after a hypo. The patient with type 1 diabetes still needs their basal insulin — omit it and you trade a hypo for ketoacidosis. The correct response is to treat the hypo, then review and adjust the regimen (usually reduce the offending dose), not to stop background insulin. Short-acting doses around the event may be delayed or reduced, but background insulin continues.

⚠️ Stopping basal insulin after a hypo can cause DKA

In type 1 diabetes there must always be background insulin on board. The knee-jerk "hold all insulin" after a hypo is how a hypo becomes tomorrow's DKA admission. Treat the low, keep the basal, adjust the dose.

Always review the cause

Every hypo is a near-miss to be investigated: missed/reduced meal, wrong dose or timing, injection-site issue, new renal impairment, deliberate/accidental overdose, alcohol, exercise, a drug interaction, or declining requirements (weight loss, resolving illness). Fix the cause or it recurs.

6 · 🚗 Driving & the DVLA — the rules you must know

Hypoglycaemia and driving is a medico-legal minefield and a favourite exam topic. The UK DVLA rules for Group 1 (car/motorcycle) drivers on insulin (and the principles extend to sulfonylureas):

  • Must have adequate awareness of hypoglycaemia, no more than one episode of severe hypoglycaemia (needing another's help) while awake in the preceding 12 months, and appropriate glucose monitoring.
  • Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia is a bar to driving until awareness is regained and confirmed.
  • Practical driving rules: check glucose within ~2 hours before driving and every 2 hours on long journeys; do not drive if glucose <5 ("5 to drive"); if a hypo occurs, stop, treat, and do not resume driving for at least 45 minutes after glucose has returned to normal (cognition lags recovery).
  • Group 2 (LGV/PCV) rules are much stricter.
💡 "5 to drive" and "45 to restart"

Glucose must be ≥5 mmol/L to start driving. After any hypo behind the wheel: stop safely, treat, and wait at least 45 minutes after normoglycaemia is restored before driving again — because the brain recovers more slowly than the blood glucose.

7 · 🛡️ Prevention — closing the loop

  • Right target for the right patient — relax targets in the frail elderly, CKD, unawareness, and those with recurrent hypos; over-tight control is a cause, not a virtue.
  • Choose safer drugs — avoid glibenclamide in the elderly/CKD; consider switching from sulfonylurea to a low-hypo-risk agent (DPP-4i, GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i) where appropriate.
  • Structured education (carbohydrate counting, DAFNE), CGM with low-glucose alarms, and pre-exercise/pre-bed carbohydrate.
  • Break the unawareness cycle — 2–3 weeks of strict hypo avoidance restores warning symptoms.
  • Provide a rescue plan — glucose tablets/gel, a home glucagon kit, and educated family.

8 · 🧾 The master treatment table

ScenarioFirst actionThenWatch for
Conscious, can swallow15–20 g fast carb, recheck at 15 minRepeat once if still <4; then long-acting carbUnder-treating; forgetting the follow-on snack
Confused, can swallowBuccal glucose gel (or IV if access)Oral carb once cooperativeAspiration if swallow unsafe
Unconscious, IV access100 mL 10% (or 200 mL 10%) / 75–100 mL 20% glucose, recheck 10 minRepeat / start 10% infusion; long-acting carb once awakeExtravasation with 50%; relapse
Unconscious, no IV accessIM glucagon 1 mgGet IV access → glucose; oral carb once ableFailure in alcohol / malnutrition / liver disease / sulfonylurea
Sulfonylurea hypo (any)Correct with IV glucoseADMIT + 10% infusion + octreotide for recurrent/overdose; monitor 24–48hDischarging early; rebound; renal accumulation
Type 1, post-hypoTreat the lowContinue basal insulin; adjust offending dose; review causeReflexly omitting basal → DKA
☠️ M&M — the sulfonylurea hypo sent home too soon

An 82-year-old woman on glibenclamide, with an eGFR of 28, was brought to the ED at 14:00 confused with a glucose of 1.6 mmol/L. She was given 100 mL of 20% glucose, woke fully, ate lunch, and her repeat glucose at 15:00 was 8.4. She lived alone and wanted to go home; a stretched department discharged her at 16:30 with "advice to eat regularly." No one had registered that glibenclamide is long-acting, renally cleared, and that her eGFR of 28 would make it accumulate for a day or more. She was found unconscious at home the next morning by a carer; glucose 1.1 mmol/L, and she had had a prolonged seizure with an aspiration pneumonia and a hypoxic brain injury from which she never fully recovered. Lessons: (1) a single good glucose after treating a sulfonylurea hypo means nothing — the drug is still driving insulin; (2) glibenclamide + CKD is the highest-risk combination and mandates admission with a glucose infusion and frequent monitoring for 24–48h; (3) octreotide should have been given to switch off the insulin drive; (4) the social factor (lives alone) made discharge even less defensible. The department treated the number on the meter, not the pharmacology in the patient.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Match the route to the conscious level: can-swallow → 15–20 g fast carb (15:15 rule) then long-acting carb; confused-but-swallowing → buccal gel; unconscious + IV → 100–200 mL 10% (or 20%) glucose; unconscious + no IV → IM glucagon.
  2. Avoid 50% glucose (sclerosant); prefer 10% and move to a titrated 10% infusion if glucose won't stay up.
  3. Glucagon fails when the liver has no glycogen — alcohol, malnutrition, liver disease — and is a poor choice in sulfonylurea hypo (may stimulate more insulin).
  4. The sulfonylurea trap: prolonged, recurrent hypos → admit, IV glucose infusion, and OCTREOTIDE to suppress insulin secretion. Never discharge because it "responded".
  5. Do not reflexively omit basal insulin after a hypo in type 1 diabetes — you'll cause DKA. Treat the low, keep the basal, adjust the dose, review the cause.
  6. DVLA: "5 to drive", check every 2h on long journeys, and don't drive for ≥45 min after a hypo is corrected; impaired awareness bars driving.

moderatorQs.q: Take us through the hypoglycaemia treatment ladder by conscious level, including doses.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It's dictated by whether the patient can safely swallow. Conscious and able to swallow: give 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. 150–200 mL fruit juice, 4–5 glucose tablets), recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still <4 mmol/L, then a long-acting carbohydrate to prevent relapse. Conscious but confused/uncooperative yet able to swallow: buccal glucose gel, or IV glucose if access. Unconscious with IV access: 100 mL of 10% glucose (up to 200 mL), or 75–100 mL of 20%, recheck at 10 minutes and repeat — avoid 50% because it's a sclerosant. Unconscious with no IV access: IM glucagon 1 mg as a bridge, then obtain access and give glucose. Once recovered, always follow fast carbohydrate with a longer-acting carbohydrate.

moderatorQs.q: Why is octreotide the specific treatment for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia, and why can IV glucose alone be self-defeating?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Sulfonylureas close the β-cell KATP channel and force glucose-independent insulin secretion, and the drug (± active metabolites, worse in renal impairment) persists for many hours — so the insulin drive continues long after you correct the glucose. The paradox is that giving IV glucose raises the glucose, which further stimulates the sulfonylurea-primed β-cell to release even more insulin — you end up chasing recurrent hypos. Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, directly suppresses pancreatic insulin secretion (e.g. 50–100 micrograms SC 8–12 hourly), breaking the loop at its source and markedly reducing rebound hypos and glucose requirements. So glucose corrects the number, octreotide treats the cause. These patients also need admission with a titrated 10% glucose infusion and monitoring for 24–48h (longer in CKD) — never discharge because a single reading improved.

moderatorQs.q: A ward junior wants to stop all insulin after a type 1 patient has a hypo. What's your guidance?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Treat the hypo, but do not stop the basal insulin. A person with type 1 diabetes has no endogenous insulin and must always have background insulin on board; if you omit it you simply trade the hypo for diabetic ketoacidosis within hours. The correct approach is to correct the low with fast carbohydrate (or IV glucose), continue the basal insulin, sensibly reduce or delay the specific short-acting dose implicated, and then review the cause — missed meal, wrong dose, exercise, new renal impairment — and adjust the regimen to prevent recurrence. 'Hold all insulin' is a knee-jerk that causes real harm.

audienceQs.q: In an unconscious hypo with no IV access I gave IM glucagon and nothing happened. What went wrong?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Glucagon works only by mobilising hepatic glycogen, so it fails whenever the liver's glycogen store is empty or the response is blunted — classically alcohol excess, malnutrition/starvation, and liver disease — and it's a poor choice in sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia because it can actually stimulate further insulin release. It also can't be repeated usefully (one dose exhausts the store). The answer is not a second shot of glucagon — it's to get IV access and give 10% glucose (100–200 mL, then an infusion if needed). Always find out what caused the hypo: an alcoholic or cachectic patient needs glucose, not glucagon.

audienceQs.q: One of our patients on gliclazide with an eGFR of 25 keeps having hypos. What should we flag to the team?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Flag that renally-cleared sulfonylureas accumulate in CKD and prolong the insulin drive, so this patient is at high risk of recurrent, prolonged hypoglycaemia — and that the kidney's own contribution to gluconeogenesis is reduced, a double hit. Recommend the team stop or substantially reduce the sulfonylurea (glibenclamide should be avoided outright in CKD/elderly; gliclazide is preferable but still risky at this eGFR), consider switching to a low-hypo-risk agent such as a DPP-4 inhibitor (dose-adjusted) or a GLP-1 receptor agonist, and relax the glycaemic target given frailty/renal impairment. Any acute severe hypo on a sulfonylurea in CKD warrants admission, a glucose infusion, and consideration of octreotide.

audienceQs.q: What exactly do I tell a patient about driving after they've had a hypo?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Use the two rules. '5 to drive': glucose must be ≥5 mmol/L before driving; if it's 4–5, take a snack first, and check within 2 hours of setting off and every 2 hours on long journeys, carrying fast carbohydrate in the car. If a hypo happens while driving: stop as soon as safe, remove the keys, treat, and do not resume for at least 45 minutes after the glucose is back to normal, because thinking recovers more slowly than the blood sugar. Advise that one episode of severe hypoglycaemia (needing help) while awake, or impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, must be reported to the DVLA and may mean stopping driving until it's resolved; Group 2 (lorry/bus) rules are stricter still.
